content: In healthcare facilities, the availability of basic services is often insufficient to meet the ambitious goals required for optimal health outcomes. The World Health Organization (WHO) Service Availability and Readiness Assessment, along with other tools such as the World Bank Service Delivery Indicators and USAID Service Provision Assessment, provide frameworks for evaluating these services. Institutions like Johns Hopkins University and Columbia University have also contributed to the development of tools and research aimed at improving maternal health and reducing disability. Healthcare facilities are inherently complex environments, offering a wide range of services that vary significantly depending on the type and size of the facility. These range from small rural primary health centers providing outpatient care to large tertiary hospitals offering specialized inpatient services. The provision of safe and high-quality care requires essential infrastructure, such as electricity and water, which are beyond the scope of this document but remain critical for service delivery. Water, sanitation, and hygiene (WASH) services are delivered in diverse contexts within healthcare facilities, and the standards for these services vary accordingly. This document outlines generic questions to assess the availability of basic WASH services across all healthcare facilities. However, additional questions may be necessary to evaluate WASH services in specialized areas, such as delivery rooms. For instance, specific indicators and questions tailored to the requirements of WASH in delivery rooms are under development to complement the generic facility-level indicators. The quality of care, including effective infection prevention and control (IPC) practices, must also be addressed to enhance the impact of WASH services on health outcomes, particularly during childbirth. Measures such as hand hygiene and environmental cleaning are integral to this document and align with the WHO Guidelines on Core Components of IPC Programs (2016) and the Infection Prevention and Control Assessment Framework (2018). Core indicators for monitoring WASH in healthcare facilities, as outlined in the Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs), define basic service levels for water, sanitation, hygiene, healthcare waste management, and environmental cleaning. These indicators provide measurable approximations of normative ideal service levels and are applicable across all types and sizes of facilities, from primary to tertiary care. They are generally applied at the facility level rather than specific locations within a facility. Basic Water Services: A healthcare facility is considered to have basic water services if its primary water source is an improved source located on the premises, with water available on the day of the survey. Improved water sources include piped water, boreholes, protected wells, protected springs, rainwater, and packaged or delivered water. The water must be accessible within the facility grounds or buildings. Basic Sanitation Services: Facilities must have improved and usable sanitation facilities, including at least one toilet dedicated to staff, one sex-separated toilet with menstrual hygiene facilities, and one toilet accessible to individuals with limited mobility. Improved sanitation facilities are designed to hygienically separate human excreta from contact and include flush/pour-flush toilets connected to sewer systems, septic tanks, or pit latrines, as well as ventilated improved pit latrines and composting toilets. Basic Hygiene Services: Functional hand hygiene facilities must be available at points of care and within 5 meters of toilets. Hand hygiene facilities include sinks with taps, water tanks with taps, or alcohol-based hand rub dispensers. For these facilities to be considered functional, they must provide soap and water or alcohol-based hand rubs at points of care. However, alcohol-based hand rubs are not sufficient for hand hygiene near toilets, as they do not remove fecal matter. Basic Healthcare Waste Management Services: Facilities must safely segregate waste in consultation areas and ensure that sharps and infectious wastes are treated and disposed of safely. This includes the use of clearly labeled or color-coded bins for sharps, infectious waste, and non-infectious general waste. Sharps containers must be puncture-proof, and bins for infectious waste must be leak-proof and have lids. Safe treatment and disposal methods include incineration, autoclaving, and burial in lined, protected pits. Alternatively, waste may be transported off-site for medical waste treatment and disposal. Basic Environmental Cleaning Practices: Facilities must have cleaning protocols in place, and all staff with cleaning responsibilities must receive training on cleaning procedures. Protocols should include step-by-step techniques for specific tasks, such as cleaning floors, sinks, and spills of blood or body fluids. A cleaning roster or schedule specifying the frequency of cleaning tasks should also be maintained. The document emphasizes the importance of progressive realization of SDG criteria through service ladders, which allow countries at different stages of development to track and compare progress. These ladders include three levels: no service, limited service, and basic service. For countries where basic service is not sufficiently ambitious, an additional advanced service level should be defined, with national criteria tailored to the specific context and type of facility. Core questions for monitoring WASH in healthcare facilities are presented in five sections: water, sanitation, hygiene, healthcare waste management, and environmental cleaning. These questions are designed to guide survey and questionnaire development, ensuring that data collection tools can effectively report on the SDG indicators. Where feasible, response options and terminology should be adapted to reflect the local context, and visual aids such as photos may be used to enhance understanding. Effective functioning of healthcare facilities and the prevention of infection spread rely on a safe, sufficient, and reliable water supply on the premises. Assessing the adequacy of a facility's water supply requires measurements of quantity, quality, and reliability, as well as consideration of different water types for various purposes.
